entry: City in northern [[Nigeria]], capital of Kano State. Nigeria's second-largest city after [[Lagos]], it has over four million residents within 449 sq km (173 sq mi). Located in the [[Savanna]] south of the [[Sahel]], Kano has been a major route of the [[Trans-Saharan trade]] for millennia. The Dabo dynasty has ruled the city as emirs since the 19th century, and the Kano Emirate Council remains the traditional institution inside the city boundaries, under the authority of the Kano State government. Kano is one of the seven medieval [[Hausa Kingdoms|Hausa kingdoms]]. Its principal inhabitants are the Hausa and Fulani, and Hausa is spoken as a [[Lingua franca|lingua franca]] by over 70 million speakers in the region. [[Islam]] arrived in the 11th century or earlier, primarily through the trans-Saharan trade, and made Kano the wealthy commercial center of northern Nigeria.

Metropolis in [[Uttar Pradesh]], India, formerly anglicized as Cawnpore. Founded by the Rajput ruler Hindu Singh Chandel, it became one of the most important commercial and military stations of the [[British Raj]]. The [[East India Company]] developed an indigo trade on the [[Ganges]], and the Grand Trunk Road (1832) and roads to [[Lucknow]] and Kalpi (1864) spurred its growth. The British garrison had barracks for 7,000 soldiers. During the [[Indian Rebellion of 1857]], rebels under Nana Sahib besieged about 900 British men, women and children for 22 days. After the British surrendered on the promise of safe passage, they were fired on at Sati Chaura Ghat, and many were killed. Kanpur is India's 12th most populous city (2011 census).

Landlocked Midwestern state on the [[Great Plains]], near the geographic center of the contiguous United States (pop., 2020: 2,940,865). It borders [[Nebraska]], [[Colorado]], [[Oklahoma]] and [[Missouri]]. Its capital is Topeka, and its most populous city is Wichita. Opened to settlement in 1854, it became the site of conflict over slavery known as Bleeding Kansas, and it entered the Union as a free state on January 29, 1861. As of 2015 it was among the most productive agricultural states, with high yields of wheat, corn, [[Sorghum]] and [[Soybean]]. Its highest point, Mount Sunflower, rises 4,039 feet (1,231 meters).

City in western [[Missouri]], the state's largest by population and area (pop., 2020: 508,090). Located on the [[Missouri River]] at its confluence with the Kansas River, it was founded in the 1830s as a port. Railroads and the Kansas City Stockyards made it a major transportation and livestock center as westward expansion grew. Its name was chosen to distinguish it from the territory of Kansas. The metropolitan area straddles the Missouri–Kansas state line and has 2.25 million residents. Known for Kansas City jazz and barbecue, it is home to the Kansas City Chiefs of the [[National Football League]] and the Royals of [[Major League Baseball]].

American rapper, songwriter and record producer, known as Ye. Raised in [[Chicago]] after early years in [[Atlanta]], he began as a producer for [[Jay-Z]]'s Roc-A-Fella Records before signing as a recording artist. His first two albums, *The College Dropout* (2004) and *Late Registration* (2005), received critical acclaim. The latter was the first of his eleven US *Billboard* 200 number-one albums. He has won 24 [[Grammy Awards]] and has sold 160 million records. He has been a frequent source of controversy, and from 2022 to 2025 he drew widespread condemnation for antisemitic views and support for [[Nazism]].

Special municipality in southern [[Taiwan]], the island's third most populous city. With about 2.7 million people, it covers 2,952 sq km (1,140 sq mi), making it Taiwan's largest city by area. Its territory extends from the coastal urban center into the mountainous Yushan Range. Founded in the 17th century as the trading village Tancoia, it became the economic center of southern Taiwan, with industries including steel-making, oil refining, [[Freight transport|freight transport]] and [[Shipbuilding|shipbuilding]]. The Port of Kaohsiung is the largest and busiest harbor in Taiwan, and more than 67% of the nation's export and import container volume passes through it. Kaohsiung International Airport is the second busiest in Taiwan by passengers. The Republic of China Navy's fleet headquarters is also here, and the Pier-2 Art Center and National Kaohsiung Center for the Arts aim to grow tourism and culture.

Phyllosilicate [[Clay|clay]] mineral with the composition Al₂Si₂O₅(OH)₄. Its structure has one tetrahedral sheet of silicate linked to one octahedral sheet of aluminate through shared oxygen atoms, and its layers are bonded to one another by hydrogen bonds. Kaolinite is a soft, earthy, usually white mineral produced by the chemical [[Weathering|weathering]] of [[Feldspar|feldspar]] and other aluminum silicate minerals. Rocks rich in it are called kaolin or china clay. Iron oxide can color kaolin pink, orange or red, while lower concentrations yield white, yellow or light orange. Because its layers carry no net charge, kaolinite has a low cation-exchange capacity and does not swell when wet. Kaolin is used in ceramics such as porcelain, in [[Paper|paper]] coating and filler, in paint and in [[Cosmetics|cosmetics]]. Global production was estimated at 45 million tonnes in 2021, worth US $4.24 billion.

Vedic sage and legendary founder of the Samkhya school of Hindu philosophy. Scholars disagree over whether he lived in the 7th or the 6th century BCE. He is traditionally credited with the *Samkhya-sutra*, which presents the dualistic philosophy of Samkhya, holding that the universe evolves from unconscious matter without a creator deity. Hindu texts describe him as an [[Avatar|avatar]] of [[Vishnu]], and the *Mahabharata* portrays him defending ahimsa, or non-violence. The *Baudhayana Dharmasutra* credits him with establishing the four ashrama orders of life. His influence on the Buddha and [[Buddhism]] has long been the subject of scholarly study, and many figures, places and a cow variety in [[Hinduism]] and Jainism share his name.

[[Cancer|Cancer]] that forms masses, usually painless purple lesions, on the skin, in lymph nodes, mouth or other organs. Except in classic cases, it is caused by a combination of immune suppression, such as [[HIV/AIDS]], and infection by human herpesvirus 8. Classic cases tend to affect older men in regions where the virus is common, while endemic cases are most common in sub-Saharan Africa. Over 35% of people with AIDS may be affected. Diagnosis is by [[Biopsy|tissue biopsy]]. Treatment depends on subtype and immune function, and antiretroviral therapy prevents and often treats it in people with HIV. Moritz Kaposi first described it in 1872.

Marginal sea of the [[Arctic Ocean]] north of Siberia. It lies between the [[Barents Sea]] to the west, separated by the Kara Strait and [[Novaya Zemlya]], and the Laptev Sea to the east, separated by the Severnaya Zemlya archipelago. Roughly 1,450 km (900 mi) long and 970 km (600 mi) wide, it covers about 880,000 sq km (339,770 sq mi) and has a mean depth of 110 m (360 ft). The sea is ice-bound for all but two months of the year. Its main ports are Novy Port and Dikson, and it is an important [[Fishing|fishing]] ground. The East-Prinovozemelsky field, an extension of the West Siberian Oil Basin, contains significant undeveloped [[Petroleum|petroleum]] and natural gas. The name comes from the Kara River; *kara* may derive from a Nenets word meaning "hummocked ice" or a Turkic word meaning "black."

Capital of the Pakistani province of [[Sindh]] and the country's largest city (pop., 2023: 20,300,000). Ranked as the 11th largest city in the world, it stands on the [[Arabian Sea]] coast at Pakistan's southern tip. Founded as the fortified village of Kolachi in 1729, it grew after the [[East India Company]] arrived in the mid-19th century and the British built a seaport and railways. It was Pakistan's federal capital from 1947 to 1959, before the capital moved to [[Islamabad]]. Karachi's ports handle approximately 95% of the country's foreign trade, and the city generates approximately 25% of national GDP. Migrants from across South Asia settled there after 1947. Ethnic and sectarian conflict intensified in the 1980s, as weapons arrived during the [[Soviet–Afghan War]]. After a 2013 crackdown by the Pakistan Rangers, recorded crime sharply decreased.

Mountain range in Asia spanning the borders of [[Pakistan]], [[India]] and [[China]]. It contains four of the fourteen eight-thousanders, including [[K2]], the second highest mountain on Earth, along with [[Broad Peak]], Gasherbrum I and Gasherbrum II. About 500 km (311 mi) long, it is the most glaciated place on Earth outside the polar regions. The Siachen Glacier, 76 km (47 mi) long, is the second longest glacier outside the polar regions. The range is part of a complex that includes the [[Himalayas]], the Pamir Mountains and the [[Hindu Kush]]. The name is a Turkic term meaning "black gravel," first applied to the Karakoram Pass, part of an unused trade route between Ladakh and Yarkand. European explorers entered the region in the early 19th century, and Francis Younghusband crossed the Muztagh Pass in 1887.

Desert in [[Central Asia]], the 12th largest in the world. Its name means "black sand" in Turkmen. It covers about 70 percent of [[Turkmenistan]], roughly 350,000 sq km (140,000 sq mi), and has an average population of one person per 6.5 sq km (2.5 sq mi). Rainfall is rare, at 70 to 150 mm (3 to 6 in) a year. The Karakum Canal, begun in 1954 and completed in 1958, carries water 1,375 km (900 mi) from the [[Amu Darya]] for irrigation. Oases such as Mary and Tejen grow [[Cotton|cotton]]. The Darvaza gas crater, burning since 1971, is known locally as the "Door to Hell." The desert has significant [[Natural gas|natural gas]] and [[Petroleum|oil]] deposits. Since the early 1980s the Aralkum, a desert extension, has covered much of the former seabed of the [[Aral Sea]].

Indian film producer, director and television host working in Hindi cinema. Johar leads Dharma Productions, which has launched the careers of several actors and filmmakers. He made his directorial debut with the romantic comedy-drama *Kuch Kuch Hota Hai* (1998), and later directed *My Name Is Khan* (2010). As a producer, his films include *Raazi* (2018) and *Shershaah* (2021). He has hosted the talk show *Koffee with Karan* since 2004. He has won four National Film Awards and eight Filmfare Awards, and received the Padma Shri from the [[Government of India]] in 2020.

Form of interactive entertainment in which people sing along to prerecorded instrumental versions of popular songs, usually in [[Bar (establishment)|bars]] and nightclubs. Singers use a [[Microphone|microphone]], and lyrics are typically shown on a video screen to guide them. The term combines Japanese *kara* ("empty") and *oke*, short for *ōkesutora* ("orchestra"). Precursor machines using cassette tapes appeared in [[Japan]] and the [[Philippines]] in the 1970s. Commercial machines using [[LaserDisc]], made by Japanese companies, spread worldwide in the 1980s. The invention is disputed: Daisuke Inoue of Japan and Roberto del Rosario of the Philippines are each credited, and only del Rosario held a patent. In Chinese-speaking countries and regions, a karaoke box is called a KTV. The global karaoke market has been estimated at nearly $10 billion.

Martial art developed in the Ryukyu Kingdom, now [[Okinawa Prefecture|Okinawa]], Japan. It developed from indigenous Ryukyuan [[Martial arts|martial arts]] called *te* under the influence of [[Chinese martial arts]]. After samurai rule banned Ryukyuans from carrying swords, young aristocrats created unarmed combat methods as a form of resistance. Karate was introduced to mainland Japan in the Taishō era (1912–1926) by Ankō Itosu and his students Gichin Funakoshi and Motobu Chōki. Funakoshi borrowed elements of [[Judo]], such as training uniforms, colored belts and ranking systems. The name changed from 唐手 ("Chinese hand") to 空手 ("empty hand") during the rise of [[Militarism]] in Japan. After World War II, karate spread through American servicemen stationed in Okinawa and, through martial arts films, around the world. It was featured at the 2020 Summer Olympics.

American family prominent in entertainment, [[Reality television|reality television]], fashion and business. Several members have assets exceeding $1 billion. The patriarch, attorney Robert Kardashian, was one of [[O. J. Simpson]]'s lawyers in the 1994 murder case. The family gained wide recognition in 2007, after a video featuring [[Kim Kardashian]] and Ray J was released. The series *Keeping Up with the Kardashians* (2007–2021) gave each member media exposure, and members built separate brands in multiple businesses. Spin-offs followed, and the family returned in *The Kardashians* (2022).

American former professional [[Basketball|basketball]] center. He played 20 seasons in the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], six with the Milwaukee Bucks and 14 with the [[Los Angeles Lakers]]. At UCLA he won three consecutive national championships. Using his trademark skyhook shot, he won a record six NBA Most Valuable Player awards, was a 19-time All-Star and was a member of six NBA championship teams as a player. He broke the NBA's career scoring record in 1984 and held it until 2023. After retiring in 1989 he worked as an actor, coach and author, having trained in Jeet Kune Do under [[Bruce Lee]]. In 2016 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from [[Barack Obama]].

Indian film actress and a leading lady of Hindi cinema since 2000. After her debut in *Refugee* (2000), a turning point came with the against-type role in *Chameli* (2004). She won a Filmfare Award for Best Actress for the romantic comedy *Jab We Met* (2007). Her highest-grossing releases include *3 Idiots* (2009) and *Bajrangi Bhaijaan* (2015). She has won six Filmfare Awards, and as of 2024 she is among Hindi cinema's highest-paid actresses. She has worked with [[UNICEF]] since 2014 to advocate for girls' education. She is the younger sister of [[Karisma Kapoor]] and is married to [[Saif Ali Khan]].

Danish author who wrote in Danish and English, known internationally as Isak Dinesen. A native of Rungstedlund, north of [[Copenhagen]], she is best known for *Out of Africa* (1937), a memoir of her years running a coffee farm near [[Nairobi]] in Kenya, and for the story "Babette's Feast." Both were adapted as films that won [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]]. Her other works include *Seven Gothic Tales* (1934) and *Winter's Tales* (1942), which blend [[Romanticism|romanticism]], irony and fatalism. She also wrote under the names Tania Blixen, Osceola and Pierre Andrézel. Postcolonial critics have questioned how her work portrays colonial Africa. She was considered several times for the Nobel Prize in Literature but did not win.

Conflict between India and [[Pakistan]] fought from May to July 1999 in the Kargil district of Ladakh, along the Line of Control. Pakistani troops disguised as Kashmiri militants had infiltrated strategic positions on the Indian side. The Indian Army, supported by the Indian Air Force, recaptured most of them through [[Artillery|artillery]] barrages and [[Infantry|infantry]] assaults. Under international diplomatic pressure, Pakistani forces withdrew from the remaining positions. India calls its military operation Operation Vijay. It was one of only two major conventional wars between nuclear-armed states.

Indian actress who primarily appears in Hindi films. One of the leading and highest-paid actresses of the 1990s, she debuted in *Prem Qaidi* (1991). Her hits included *Raja Hindustani* (1996), which won her a Filmfare Award for Best Actress, and *Dil To Pagal Hai* (1997), for which she won the National Film Award for Best Supporting Actress. She won Filmfare Awards for *Fiza* (2000) and *Zubeidaa* (2001). Sister of [[Kareena Kapoor]], she was married to businessman Sanjay Kapur from 2003 to 2016. She has appeared only sporadically since taking a sabbatical in 2004.

Swiss Reformed theologian whose critique of liberal Protestantism reshaped twentieth-century theology. His commentary *The Epistle to the Romans* (first edition 1919, second edition 1921) portrayed God as wholly other and broke with liberal theology. He pastored in Safenwil from 1911 to 1921, then taught at Göttingen, Münster and [[Bonn]]. He was deported from Germany in 1935 after refusing to sign an unmodified oath of loyalty to [[Adolf Hitler]], and taught at [[Basel]] until 1962. A leader of the Confessing Church, he wrote most of the Barmen Declaration of 1934. His unfinished multi-volume *Church Dogmatics* (1932–1967) is his major work. He was featured on the cover of [[Time (magazine)|Time]] in 1962.

German naval officer who briefly succeeded [[Adolf Hitler]] as head of state after Hitler's suicide in April 1945. In World War I he began developing the *Rudeltaktik*, or wolfpack, concept of U-boats attacking in groups. At the start of World War II he led the [[U-boat]] arm, and from 1943 he commanded the navy as Grand Admiral, becoming the main enemy of Allied shipping in the [[Battle of the Atlantic]]. He headed the Flensburg Government until the Allies dissolved it in May 1945. At the [[Nuremberg trials]] he was convicted of crimes against peace and war crimes, and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment.

American former power forward in the [[National Basketball Association|National Basketball Association]]. He played 18 seasons, mostly with the Utah Jazz, and reached the NBA Finals in 1997 and 1998, losing both times to the [[Chicago Bulls]]. He scored 36,928 career points, third in NBA history, and holds the records for most free throws made and attempted. He won Olympic gold medals with the U.S. national team in 1992 and 1996 and was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2010. His conduct drew criticism after it emerged that he impregnated a 13-year-old while attending Louisiana Tech; no statutory rape charges were filed.
